data.title: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) Secures Injunction Delaying Simponi Biosimilar Launch
data.description:
• Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) unit Janssen secured a preliminary injunction that delays Alvotech's proposed Simponi biosimilar launch in the U.S.
  • The injunction preserves Janssen's Simponi position while patent and regulatory claims with Alvotech proceed through U.S. courts.
  • Johnson & Johnson also received expanded FDA clearance for its HARMONIC 1100 Shears to cover ENT surgical procedures.
  • Janssen's Simponi biosimilar injunction and the broader HARMONIC 1100 Shears clearance deserve a fresh look in the context of Johnson & Johnson's full risk picture. Ask Charlie what the 2 warning signs mean for HARMONIC 1100 Shears FDA clearance.

For readers scanning beyond Johnson & Johnson for more ideas in surgical automation and related tools, start with 93 robotics and automation stocks.

Johnson & Johnson operates as a diversified healthcare group that develops medicines, medical devices, and consumer health products worldwide, so the Simponi patent dispute and the HARMONIC 1100 Shears decision both sit squarely in its core pharmaceuticals and surgical tools activities.

3 things going right for Johnson & Johnson that this headline doesn't cover.

How this Simponi ruling and device clearance really affect the Johnson & Johnson story

Johnson & Johnson’s Narrative leans on drug franchises in immunology and oncology while MedTech rebuilds credibility, so a Simponi biosimilar delay and a broader HARMONIC 1100 Shears label speak directly to how durable that mix can be.

"Ongoing expansion within MedTech, highlighted by strong performance from acquired cardiovascular units Abiomed and Shockwave, as well as developments in robotic surgery, are expected to drive revenue growth and enhance adjusted income margins over time…"

See how the full story points towards a $279 fair value for Johnson & Johnson.

The Simponi injunction effectively buys Janssen more time in a therapy area where biosimilar competition is a key Narrative risk, especially after loss of exclusivity on older drugs like STELARA. It supports the part of the story that says next generation medicines and legal defenses can keep immunology cash flows steadier while newer assets like TREMFYA and CAPLYTA build out.

The HARMONIC 1100 Shears ENT clearance pulls in the opposite direction to recent concerns around MedTech underperformance, since it broadens the procedure set J&J can serve in surgical energy just as OTTAVA begins its roll out against players like Intuitive Surgical and Medtronic. That said, analysts have already flagged margin pressure and execution slip ups, so these approvals look more like necessary proof points than a clean reset for the segment.

The upshot is that the same injunction and device win can either reinforce a thesis about resilient cash generators or underline how hard Johnson & Johnson has to work just to keep its bigger earnings story on track.

data.title: Only Three Days Left To Cash In On Texas Pacific Land's (NYSE:TPL) Dividend
data.description:
Readers hoping to buy Texas Pacific Land Corporation (NYSE:TPL) for its dividend will need to make their move shortly, as the stock is about to trade ex-dividend. The ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. It is important to be aware of the ex-dividend date because any trade on the stock needs to have been settled on or before the record date. Therefore, if you purchase Texas Pacific Land's shares on or after the 1st of December, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 15th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.60 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$2.40 to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Texas Pacific Land has a trailing yield of 0.9% on the current stock price of US$261.37. We love seeing companies pay a dividend, but it's also important to be sure that laying the golden eggs isn't going to kill our golden goose! As a result, readers should always check whether Texas Pacific Land has been able to grow its dividends, or if the dividend might be cut.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Dividends are typically paid out of company income, so if a company pays out more than it earned, its dividend is usually at a higher risk of being cut. Fortunately Texas Pacific Land's payout ratio is modest, at just 27% of profit. Yet cash flow is typically more important than profit for assessing dividend sustainability, so we should always check if the company generated enough cash to afford its dividend. Over the past year it paid out 136% of its free cash flow as dividends, which is uncomfortably high. It's hard to consistently pay out more cash than you generate without either borrowing or using company cash, so we'd wonder how the company justifies this payout level.

Texas Pacific Land paid out less in dividends than it reported in profits, but unfortunately it didn't generate enough cash to cover the dividend. Were this to happen repeatedly, this would be a risk to Texas Pacific Land's ability to maintain its dividend.

See our latest analysis for Texas Pacific Land

Click here to see how much of its profit Texas Pacific Land paid out over the last 12 months.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Stocks in companies that generate sustainable earnings growth often make the best dividend prospects, as it is easier to lift the dividend when earnings are rising. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. It's encouraging to see Texas Pacific Land has grown its earnings rapidly, up 28% a year for the past five years. Earnings have been growing quickly, but we're concerned dividend payments consumed most of the company's cash flow over the past year.

Another key way to measure a company's dividend prospects is by measuring its historical rate of dividend growth. Since the start of our data, 10 years ago, Texas Pacific Land has lifted its dividend by approximately 53% a year on average. It's exciting to see that both earnings and dividends per share have grown rapidly over the past few years.

To Sum It Up

Should investors buy Texas Pacific Land for the upcoming dividend? We like that Texas Pacific Land has been successfully growing its earnings per share at a nice rate and reinvesting most of its profits in the business. However, we note the high cashflow payout ratio with some concern. It might be worth researching if the company is reinvesting in growth projects that could grow earnings and dividends in the future, but for now we're not all that optimistic on its dividend prospects.

With that in mind, a critical part of thorough stock research is being aware of any risks that stock currently faces. For example, we've found 1 warning sign for Texas Pacific Land that we recommend you consider before investing in the business.

The Bottom Line

  • The proposed US-backed restrictions highlight how concentrated ASML Holding's demand is in China for immersion DUV equipment and services, raising practical questions about revenue mix, pricing power and supply planning as management already reports that planned 2027 and 2028 production will not fully meet customer orders.

ASML Holding Investment Narrative Recap

To own ASML Holding, you need to believe its lithography tools remain essential for leading chipmakers and that capacity additions are absorbed by customer roadmaps for AI, logic and memory. The immediate operational catalyst is management’s raised 2026 sales guidance to €44–45b and higher margin targets, which anchor orders and factory loading despite recent share price volatility.

The biggest risk right now sits in policy rather than engineering. MATCH Act pressure on China shipments could alter ASML Holding’s revenue mix and pricing for immersion DUV tools, although management currently frames China export controls as more about timing and price than overall volume, given demand that already exceeds planned 2027–2028 supply.

One announcement that ties directly into this is management’s plan to expand immersion DUV capacity by about 30% for 2027, highlighted by Ivoed, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the Narrative. data.title: Why Did A Coherent (COHR) Director Triple Their Stake?
data.description:
• Independent director Stephen Pagliuca bought $34.7m of Coherent (NYSE:COHR) stock on November 24, 2026, increasing his holding to roughly three times its previous size.
  • Over twelve months, three insiders bought and six insiders sold, with trading tilting towards the buyers.

Coherent’s recent insider activity shows directors committing additional personal capital to the business. For investors who want to see where other corporate leaders are also buying shares with their own money, it is worth reviewing 70 undervalued small caps that insiders are buying.

Coherent insiders are pulling in different directions

Stephen Pagliuca has been the clear outlier at Coherent, committing fresh capital while several board colleagues have been trimming their exposure. Independent Non-Employee Directors Joseph Corasanti and Enrico Digirolamo both reduced their holdings over the past year, with Corasanti cutting his stake by 16% and Digirolamo reducing his by 27% across a run of sales. The shares now trade 33% below Digirolamo's average sale price, a drop that person avoided on the stock sold, while Corasanti's trades line up with a price that is close to where the shares change hands today.

Pagliuca's activity has gone the other way. The November 2026 purchase followed earnings early that month that set out how the business had been trading, and the shares have since stayed close to the level where Pagliuca and the other buyers paid in. The November move was also the second open market purchase from Pagliuca in a year, so it reads more as a run of buying than a one off. Taken together, these filings show non-employee directors split between one heavyweight buyer and a couple of measured sellers. This points more to mixed conviction than a clear shared signal.

AI optics demand has to translate into durable high margin Coherent revenue

For Stephen Pagliuca’s November 24, 2026 buying to work, Coherent needs its AI optics push to show up in sustained high margin business rather than a short spike. The November 19, 2026 repurchase plan points to the board committing capital at roughly the same price, and the stock sitting around the insiders’ levels means that test is still open.

Coherent now needs AI datacenter and high performance computing buildouts to keep pulling in record Datacenter & Communications orders with long visibility. Internal manufacturing projects, including extra indium phosphide lines, have to deliver scale and a leaner cost base that supports better profitability. PhotonLink and higher value datacenter interconnect products then need to ramp on those contracts so revenue mix supports the margin targets set out in COHR: AI Optics Demand Was The Hook, Order Visibility And Margins Drive The Case.

The insiders have made their call. Now find out what Coherent could be worth.

Insider trades sit on a typical base

Several insiders bought Coherent shares with their own money, and the register shows how much of the company they share in. Insiders together hold 0.3% of the company, worth $126.6m at today’s price, which is typical for a company this size. Their trades come from people with a material personal exposure, but not from owners who control where most of the equity sits.

Insiders’ buying and selling at Coherent reflects meaningful personal positioning, but it does not appear to be the kind of activity that reshapes who really owns the stock.

We count open-market transactions and private dispositions of directly held shares only, not derivative transactions such as option exercises or interests held indirectly, for example through a family trust or company.
